commits.messageBody:
Adding .gitkeep for PR creation (default mode).
This file will be removed when the task is complete.

Issue: https://github.com/link-assistant/hive-mind/issues/2156

A `gho_` GitHub token was published in an attached log and revoked by
GitHub secret scanning. Two independent defects let it through, each
reproduced against the pre-fix tree in
experiments/issue-2156-reproduce-before-fix.mjs:

1. Base64-encoded credential. The agent ran `gh auth token`, base64'd it
   for an `Authorization: Basic` header and POSTed to ghcr.io/token.
   GHCR echoes the PAT back base64-encoded in the JSON response body.
   Every sanitizer layer compared bytes literally, so the encoded copy
   walked straight through. GitHub's scanner decodes before matching,
   which is exactly why the token was revoked.

2. Backslash-escaped JSON quoting. Agent tool results embed stdout as a
   JSON string, so the log bytes are `{\"token\":\"...\"}`. The quoted /
   unquoted assignment rules could not match through the escapes.

New src/encoded-credential-detection.lib.mjs decodes bounded base64,
base64url, hex, percent, byte-escape and HTML-entity runs, re-runs the
existing plaintext rules over the decoded text, then re-encodes and
verifies the round trip before substituting. Non-secret payload content
and the first/last-character debug window are preserved; a failed round
trip degrades to whole-run redaction. Base64 also matches at all three
byte alignments so a credential embedded mid-blob is still found.

Also:
- credential-sanitization-core: escape-aware quoting, semver carve-out,
  encoded-aware sanitizeCredentialText (findCredentialResiduals inherits
  it, so the fail-closed publication check covers encoded forms).
- token-sanitization: mask known-local tokens in their encoded forms in
  sanitizeOutput and sanitizeCommentBody; containsKnownToken now reports
  the encoding that matched.

Verified on the real 17MB / 120,277-line log: leak gone, idempotent,
6 changed lines, all genuine token fields, zero false positives.
Tests use synthetic tokens only — the leaked value is never stored here.
commits.messageHeadline: fix(security): detect credentials that only appear re-encoded (#2156)

commits.messageBody:
…alls (#2156)

`postKillRecoveryNotice()` assembled a pull request comment from kill
diagnostics and a resume command, wrote it to a temp file, and posted it
with `runCommand('gh', ['pr', 'comment', url, '--body-file', bodyFile])`
without ever sanitizing the body. Every other publication boundary in the
codebase fails closed through `sanitizeForPublication`; this one did not.

The reason it stayed unsanitized is that the `require-sanitized-output`
ESLint rule only understood shell strings and tagged templates. An argv
array carries no shell text, so the rule was structurally blind to it.

Both halves are fixed:

* `postKillRecoveryNotice()` now sanitizes the body before writing it.
* The rule now recognises `gh` invocations whose arguments are an array,
  flagging a publishing subcommand (issue/pr/gist/release + create/
  comment/edit/review) whose `--body`/`--body-file`/`--title`/`--notes`/
  `--comment` value is not provably sanitized. It also tracks file
  writers (`writeFile`/`writeFileSync`/`outputFile`) so a sanitized write
  marks the path safe and a later raw write un-marks it, and tracks array
  destructuring from `Promise.all([...])` so each name inherits the
  sanitization status of its own element.

Verified by negative control: reverting the one-line fix makes the rule
report `src/session-kill-recovery.lib.mjs`; restoring it is clean.

commits.messageBody:
Every base64 wrapper in common use folds its output — base64(1) and MIME at
76 columns, PEM and openssl at 64 — and a folded blob has no single-line run,
so the encoded detector added for this issue never saw it. That is a third
evasion class alongside plain base64 and escaped JSON.

Detection scans contiguous groups of base64-only lines and expands outward
over the partial line the blob started on and the remainder line it ends on.
Two ambiguities are resolved rather than guessed:

  - A preceding line made only of base64 characters (a bare word, a path) is
    indistinguishable from a real `body=<segment>` prefix, and absorbing one
    that does not belong misaligns the fold so the payload decodes to noise
    and nothing is detected. Both readings are offered as candidates; the one
    that actually decodes wins.

  - A short following line is equally ambiguous, and absorbing it deletes it
    from the log. `=` padding proves the payload is already complete, a total
    length that is not a multiple of 4 cannot complete it, and anything that
    lowers printability is rejected. `done`, `OK` and `tail` all survive.

The stream sanitizer holds a trailing group of base64-only lines back until a
line that cannot belong to the blob arrives, the way an unterminated PEM block
is already held; releasing them one at a time hands the sanitizer byte-
misaligned slices. Ordinary records — including the URL- and path-heavy lines
this tool prints — are still released by the write that completes them.

Also bounds `SENSITIVE_KEY`, whose unbounded affixes made the assignment rules
retry from every offset of a long unbroken run: 64 KB took 38 s and a 553 KB
blob never finished. Publication sanitizes before it releases anything, so
that was a hang on the fail-closed path, not a slowdown. Now 137 ms.

Verified against the 17 MB incident log: same 6 changed lines as before, still
idempotent, line count preserved.
